record.original_question: What performance metrics are most suitable for fairly comparing nature-inspired optimization algorithms, and is it possible to design a unified framework that compares all such algorithms both fairly and rigorously?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 4. What are the most suitable performance metrics for fairly comparing all algorithms? Is it possible to design a unified framework to compare all algorithms fairly and rigorously.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the class N of nature-inspired (meta)heuristic optimization algorithms, i.e., iterative stochastic procedures A that, given a black-box objective function f : X → R on a search space X (typically X ⊆ R^n or a discrete combinatorial domain), produce a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, … ∈ X aimed at approximating arg min_{x ∈ X} f(x). Examples include genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution, simulated annealing, ant colony optimization, cuckoo search, firefly algorithm, and similar population-based or trajectory-based heuristics.

A performance metric is a functional M that, given an algorithm A ∈ N, a benchmark distribution or set of test problems F = {f_1, …, f_K}, a computational budget B (e.g., maximum number of function evaluations), and a probabilistic model of A's randomness, assigns a real number M(A; F, B) measuring quality (e.g., expected best-so-far value, success rate to reach a target, expected runtime, anytime performance, convergence rate, robustness across problem instances, or computational complexity per iteration).

A comparison framework is a tuple (F, B, M, S) consisting of a benchmark family F, a budget specification B, one or more metrics M, and a statistical decision procedure S that, on the basis of finitely many independent runs of each algorithm, outputs a (possibly partial) ranking of any finite subset of N.

Problems:
(1) Identify performance metrics M that are most suitable for fairly comparing arbitrary algorithms A, A' ∈ N, where 'fair' requires at minimum that M be invariant under cosmetic reformulations of an algorithm (renaming, trivial reparameterizations), account for per-iteration computational cost, control for tuning effort and the No-Free-Lunch constraint that average performance over all functions is identical for all algorithms, and provide statistically rigorous (e.g., distribution-free) guarantees from a finite number of runs.
(2) Determine whether there exists a single unified comparison framework (F, B, M, S) that, applied to every pair A, A' ∈ N, yields rankings that are fair in the above sense and rigorous in the sense of admitting provable statistical or complexity-theoretic guarantees; or, alternatively, prove that no such unified framework can exist (e.g., by an impossibility theorem analogous to No-Free-Lunch or to Arrow-type results).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem about benchmarking methodology for nature-inspired optimization algorithms. While benchmarking suites (BBOB/COCO, CEC, IOHprofiler) and statistical comparison protocols (Demšar-style nonparametric tests, fixed-budget vs. fixed-target analyses) are widely used and continue to be refined, no unified, universally accepted "fair and rigorous" framework comparing all metaheuristics has been established; the metaheuristics community continues to debate fairness of comparisons, novelty of "new" nature-inspired methods, and No-Free-Lunch implications. The problem appears to remain open as a methodological/foundational question.

status_evidence.title: COCO: A Platform for Comparing Continuous Optimizers in a Black-Box Setting
status_evidence.snippet: COCO provides benchmark function suites and post-processing for comparing black-box optimizers, but is one of several competing benchmarking platforms.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple competing benchmarking platforms exist; no single unified accepted framework.

status_evidence.title: IOHprofiler: A benchmarking and profiling tool for iterative optimization heuristics
status_evidence.snippet: IOHprofiler is an alternative benchmarking environment, indicating ongoing methodological fragmentation.
status_evidence.claim: Active research on benchmarking methodology suggests the unification problem is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Lones, Mitigating metaphors: a comprehensible guide to recent nature-inspired algorithms
status_evidence.snippet: Critiques of metaphor-heavy nature-inspired algorithms argue current comparisons are often unfair and call for more rigorous standards.
status_evidence.claim: Community recognizes that fair, rigorous comparison of nature-inspired algorithms is not yet solved.
